name: Rosehip oil

lead: Rosehip oil is pressed from the seeds of wild roses such as Rosa rubiginosa and Rosa canina. It is marketed as a natural oil for scars, stretch marks and skin tone, in part because it contains unsaturated fatty acids and antioxidants.

Wikipedia describes the oil's composition and notes some research on inflammatory skin conditions with promising findings, but its page does not address scars. No scar trial of rosehip oil appears among the sources reviewed here.

paras: The oil contains linoleic, linolenic and oleic fatty acids plus tocopherols, carotenoids and phenolic compounds, and Wikipedia attributes proposed anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects to this content. A laboratory wound-healing study reported accelerated healing via macrophage changes.
The sources reviewed give no safety data. Laboratory work shows the oil is used as an ingredient in formulations and as a test subject for adulteration detection.

lead: Rosehip oil, or rose seed oil, is a vegetable oil from the seeds of wild roses, usually Rosa rubiginosa (rosa mosqueta), grown in the southern Andes, or Rosa canina [1]. It is used in cosmetics and sold with claims about scars, stretch marks and skin appearance.

Wikipedia reports that it contains the essential fatty acids linoleic and linolenic acid, the monounsaturated oleic acid, tocopherols, carotenoids and phenolic compounds, and has provitamin A, mainly beta-carotene, rather than vitamin A itself [1]. The article does not discuss scars or give safety information [1].

Published work in the sources reviewed is mostly formulation science and laboratory research, including a wound-healing study in a model of excisional wounds [2]. No published human trial of rosehip oil specifically for scars was identified.
infobox: Linoleic, linolenic and oleic acids; tocopherols; carotenoids

paras: Wikipedia lists linoleic, linolenic and oleic fatty acids, delta- and gamma-tocopherol, carotenoids and phenolic compounds as constituents, and notes that provitamin A, mostly beta-carotene, is present [1]. Spectroscopic methods have been used to characterise the oil and to detect adulteration [3][4].

Rosehip oil is applied to skin as a cosmetic oil. It has also been used as an ingredient in nanoemulsion and nanocapsule formulations, for example with kojic dipalmitate for melasma [5] and with isotretinoin and quercetin in a laboratory acne-related formulation [6]. These are formulation studies, not evidence for the oil alone.

Wikipedia reports that researchers tested topical rose hip seed oil with oral fat-soluble vitamins on inflammatory skin conditions such as eczema, with promising findings, though it flags the source as possibly unreliable [1]. A 2019 Planta Medica study reported that the oil promoted excisional wound healing by accelerating macrophage phenotypic transition [2].

No studies found on rosehip oil for scars in humans. A 2013 randomised, double-blind trial tested a specific anti-stretch-mark cream for striae gravidarum [7]; the product was a formulation and is not evidence for rosehip oil alone.
Rosehip oil is mentioned as a natural skincare option for scars. No community material is cited here.
